topic: Media, Social Networks and Critical Thinking

scenarios.context: Two friends check whether a story they saw online is true.

speakerA.en: Have you seen this article? It claims that a new law will ban all private cars in the city centre next month.
I'm not sure. It was shared by a few of my friends, so I assumed it was true.
So how can I tell whether a story is reliable?
I've just searched, and nobody else has mentioned it. There's no official statement either.
I'm a bit embarrassed. I nearly posted it on my profile.
From now on I'll verify things before sharing them.

speakerB.en: Hold on. Who published it? I've never heard of that website.
That doesn't prove anything. Fake stories often spread quickly because they're designed to shock people.
Check whether reputable news outlets are reporting the same thing, and look for the original source of the claim.
Then it's almost certainly false. Notice also that the headline uses very emotional language.
Don't be. Even experienced adults get fooled. What matters is that you stopped to question it.
Good plan. If more people did that, misinformation would spread much more slowly.

scenarios.scenario: Too much time on social media
scenarios.context: A mother and her son discuss how long he spends online.

speakerA.en: Sam, I'm worried that you spend almost five hours a day on social media. Don't you think that's excessive?
I accept that, but you've been tired and distracted lately, and your grades have dropped.
Possibly, but I'd like us to find a compromise. What if the phone stays out of your bedroom at night?
You could buy a normal alarm clock, and you could still play music downstairs while you get ready for bed.
Fair point. I hadn't noticed how often I do that. We should both be more careful.
Thank you. I'm not trying to control you. I just want you to be healthy.

speakerB.en: I understand your concern, but it's how I keep in touch with my friends. It's not just wasted time.
Maybe, but that could be because of the pressure at school rather than my phone.
That's a bit strict. I use it as an alarm clock, and I like listening to music before I fall asleep.
All right, but only if you follow the same rule. You're on your phone at dinner too.
Then I'm willing to try it for a month and see whether I sleep better.
I know, and I appreciate that. Thanks for listening instead of simply giving orders.

scenarios.context: Two students in an IT class talk about passwords and personal data.

speakerA.en: Did you read about the data leak last week? Millions of users had their passwords exposed.
That's risky. If a hacker gets one password, they can access all your accounts.
Use a password manager, and turn on two-step verification wherever possible.
In theory, yes, but the data is encrypted, so it's much safer than reusing weak passwords.
It depends on whether the app really needs it. A map does, but a simple game doesn't.
Exactly. Companies make money from your data, so the less you share, the better protected you are.

speakerB.en: I did, and it made me realise how careless I've been. I use the same password for almost everything.
What would you recommend? I can't remember dozens of different passwords.
Isn't a password manager just as vulnerable? Everything is stored in one place.
I see. What about the apps that ask for my location? Should I worry about those?
So I should review my settings and delete anything I don't use.
I'll spend this evening sorting it all out. Thanks for the advice.

scenarios.context: Two friends talk about hidden advertising on social media.

speakerA.en: I can't believe how many influencers promote products without saying they're being paid.
Exactly. My cousin bought an expensive skincare product because her favourite influencer swore by it.
Not at all. She got a rash and then discovered that the influencer had never even used it.
The problem is that the rules aren't always enforced, and young people often don't notice the small print.
I'd agree with that. Learning to question what we see would protect us from all sorts of manipulation.
True, and I don't want to generalise. I just think we should always ask who benefits from a recommendation.

speakerB.en: Some do it openly, but others make it look like a personal recommendation, which is misleading.
And did it work?
That's awful. In many countries, creators are legally required to label sponsored posts.
So perhaps we should be teaching media literacy at school, as well as maths and history.
Still, not every influencer is dishonest. Some share genuinely useful information.
That's a sensible rule for life, not only for social media.

scenarios.context: A teacher and a student discuss how two newspapers reported the same event.

speakerA.en: Today I'd like each of you to compare how two newspapers reported the same event. Has anyone started?
Interesting. Why do you think their opinions differed so much?
Exactly. Did either of them leave out important information?
So neither article gave the full picture. How would you describe the writers' tone?
Good observation. What conclusion can you draw about reading only one source?
Precisely. Reading widely is the best defence against bias.

speakerB.en: Yes, I chose the story about the new factory. One paper called it a great opportunity, while the other warned about pollution.
I suppose each paper has its own audience and its own political stance, so they emphasise different facts.
The first one didn't mention the environmental report, and the second didn't say how many jobs would be created.
The first was enthusiastic, almost like an advertisement, whereas the second was quite alarming.
That we'd end up with a one-sided view without even realising it.
I'll try to compare at least two sources from now on, even if it takes longer.
